title: This is what gamedev should be about
author: asinglebit
selftext:
Im a professional software engineer of many years. I have been doing software for over a decade and a half. My only goal in life was to learn how to make games and i taught myself math, c++, c#, javascript, rust, opengl, glsl, houdini, 3ds max, blender, unreal, zbrush, godot and unity. I know how to do professional 3d and 2dm, i have done complex character rigs, music and what not. I work as en engineer by day and do gamedev by night for many years. And now i am thrilled that ai makes all of this much easier. It has some downsides but the upsides outewigh all of them. I find it so strange that people try to gatekeep knowledge and skill. It is truly disgusting and i see it with art, coding (especially on reddit) and now math. I feel like people are unable to get past their egos and the goal was never the art per se. Of course people can use ai to do low effort stuff but that was always the case. It is much easier to steal but it is also much easier to make stuff and do good things with ai. I see it as a fair playing field.

Im writing more to vent. I loved gamedev and coding communities here on reddit. But nowadays they are full of pseudo moralists and slop. Programming communities as well. Full of opportunistic people and moralists. It seems like genuine effort gets lost and attacked.

This community is a breath of fresh air. I enjoy seeing people be creative. theres some slop here as well, but theres far more creativity than in other gamedev or art related communities. And i like the culture of sharing your wins without the ego. Good day

comments.author: lophtt

replies.author: Kyxoan7
replies.body:
They also buy a $10 game and refund it after 1:59 and then make a negative review OR they buy a $10 game, play for 6000 hours and leave a negative review saying something like "okay game, not worth $10, wait for sale for $3".

I never penny pinch when buying games I'm interested in,  I buy it, I play it for a weekend and then am usually done with it until I get an itch to do it again at a later date.  I have no remorse even for games that cost $100s of dollars like collectors packs for AAA games.

To think a dev who spent year(s) on a game, self coded or AI coded is not worth $10 is crazy to me.

replies.author: TechnicalCricket774
replies.body:
Making games is an art and art is subjective. That is why we give awards for best games of the year. 

Just cause you make something and price it at $10 doesn’t entitle you to $10. It’s still based on what a buyer perceives it’s worth to be. 

Like for example you’re OK with spending $100 on a digital good, I think that’s a bad financial decision and it’s crazy to me.

replies.author: Kyxoan7
replies.body:
Think you were missing my point entirely.

" they buy a $10 game, play for 6000 hours and leave a negative review saying something like "okay game, not worth $10, wait for sale for $3"."

If you spend 6000 hours playing a game, that means you must have been enjoying the game or are crazy, in which case, you probably need to be locked up to keep us safe.

I did not mean anywhere in my post that  "If a dev prices a game at X, they are entitled to X"  But to me the people who have no idea how to make a game and possess no skill are the same ones to criticize others and I have found this is true across ALL walks of life.  Where people have no idea how hard others work at something and have their own opinions on what something should cost.

Look at home improvement contractors, landscapers, etc.   A landscaper tries to charge $50 a week for full service lawncare (including fertilizer, seed, cleanups, dethatch, aerate) and the homeowner is like "well it only takes me an hour to cut it, its not worth $50"  meanwhile they ignore everything I listed above, on top of labor costs, insurance costs, fuel costs to drive them them and operate any equipment, licensing costs, etc.

People tend to live in bubbles and criticize others with no grasp on reality, which was my point.

replies.author: TechnicalCricket774
replies.body:
If you wanted people who know how to make games to be the ones who judge games, I’m sorry to say, you wouldn’t be in that zone. Maybe your AI would be, but without it, would you be able to make a game on you’re own?  (You 100% could it would just take time to learn) 

Also to burst you bubble, most people work over 5hrs to make $50. Most people would not be able to afford 1hr of yard work for $50. 

Also also in your analogy it would be more like this guy does 5hrs of yard work for $50 or I pay you $50 to hire someone else to do it for $10 for an hr and I need to go back to fix all the parts you missed cause you don’t know how he cut the lawn, just that he did and that was good enough for you.

replies.author: Kyxoan7
replies.body:
I'm not sure how you brought my money vs cost analogy into something about AI but cool on that point.

Most people are not working 5 hrs to make $50.  That is $10 an hour.  Very few adults are working at minimum wage (ones set at the federal cap vs a state passed one).

You are also missing the point of my $50 landscaping example.  It wasn't about being able to afford it or not afford it.  It was about the logical value a person who has no idea about running a business / being a landscaper puts on work that they don't have to do.

I couldn't care less if someone can afford or not afford something, but people put this artificial number in their head about what it takes to make or do something and use that as gospel to talk down to others.  

The entire point of my landscaping example was that it takes 2 employees of labor, gas for a truck and equipment, maintenance for the truck and equipment, insurance costs, taxes, etc to run that business that is charging you $50.  While it might take you 1 hour to do your yard and it takes the company 20 minutes to do it, you can not factor in you waking up, putting on pants and starting your lawnmower against a business.

The same can be said for game development.  You have no idea how long it took a dev to make a game, you have no idea what assets they purchased / hired someone to make or jobs they hired people to do.  Advertising costs, listing costs,  cuts from distributers, etc.

Again, I was targeting THIS TYPE OF PERSON with my comment:

"they buy a $10 game, play for 6000 hours and leave a negative review saying something like "okay game, not worth $10, wait for sale for $3"."

  
Not YOU

replies.author: zomgmeister
replies.body: I spoke about people who say this: "you should learn now to do it properly instead of making ai do it for you" - no matter how good or bad the content is. Of course the slop exist, human or AI made. That is beside the point. The point is that non-slop also exists, and it can be made by humans or by AI (well, humans+AI, but that is technicality for the purpose of the issue). Which is often ignored by prejudiced AI haters, most of which do not have skills they demand other people to have. Like "duh, why don't you learn code yourself instead of asking AI to write it all for you" is so stupid in November 2026 that there is no point to rebuke it already, and it only will became more stupid in time.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
Well, I would say, I do not know where you get the heat for AI written code, but I seen most of the games are called slop, because of design, ux, art or just quality in general.

Now there is the thing, many people who share the new wave of games are people who have no experience in programming, in art, in design, in writing, in ux. I do not say all of them, but many of them.

Now they have an idea and they try to make game from it. So basically with any knowledge about any part of game development, their share their game and after they have surprised pikachu face, when people do not like it.

I seen here people who asked about how you can generate text for your rpg, which not sounds that ai. Literally in rpg where the writing is the most important part.

I think many times the problem is that people think the ai solves all the parts of game development for them, which is not true at all, you need to have knowledge and understanding of how to make a game.

comments.author: Crafty-Following8762
comments.body:
I’m still making much of my game and its assets by hand. It wouldn’t be what I wanted any other way. I also need to know what I’m doing for my confidence’s sake. Otherwise, Claude and Chat are going to be way ahead of me and the project is out of my control.

AI has made it exponentially easier to learn the skills I need to make it all happen. There has genuinely been nothing better.

comments.author: Dicethrower
comments.body:
Absolutely. People who say AI is soulless and lacking in creation aren't creators themselves. To them the artist is as much of a blackbox as AI is, and they just hate the idea that, as far as they understand how anything works, a human is replaced.

I'm now more creative than ever. I'm no longer bogged down by the immense amount of time it takes to write code just to validate a single idea. Not only can I validate ideas quickly. I can work out 5 ideas at the same time. I went from being a (relatively) slow solo developer to having a hyper fast team of programmers under my belt. And when I say slow, I just mean as a human slow. I've often been described as the fastest developer on any team. AI is just that much faster.

Most importantly, I'm no longer reliant on others to get on my level of enthusiasm and energy. People say I'm social irl, yet in 15y I've never been able to convince anyone to get on board. I've always been stuck at studios trying to work with people too focused on making a pretty code base than getting sh\*t done. People more concerned about setting up rules and barriers under some misplaced sense of it achieving quality, rather than focusing on actually making good games.

I feel unshackled and now it's possible to make quality games that play and feel amazing, and in months rather than years. The last month specifically has been an absolute blast.

comments.author: Django_McFly
comments.body:
It's like a *Dark* loop.  I saw it in music.  Anything that makes it easier to do music than when you first got started is evil by default.  It's crazy because like most people only get in because at the time, there was some tech breakthrough that made doing music seem more realistic for everyday people like themselves.  10 years pass and now there is a new breakthrough, like nobody remembers being a teen and how breakthroughs helped them.  They just declare it evil.

I like computers but I didn't start making music on computers because I hated hardware or hated humans like the hardware people always said.  A full featured DAW was $300 and it was basically everything you'd need.  A MPC was $1500 used and it came with no sounds.  To get sounds that would be another $1500 on a Triton.  I'm a minor working minimum wage and it's illegal for me to work more than 20 hours in a week.  One was an option, the other was not.  It wasn't to destroy the world and ruin the music industry.  I just wanted to make music and this was the only way.

I feel like everyone forgets about their early years when they come out against anything new.

Like anyone who pivoted to pre-made game engines or started making games once there were premde game engines available can't really make the argument that game making needs to be maximum difficulty always.  Like they never opted for max difficulty.  They took every "shortcut" that was available at the time.  When uncs cried about it, they gave a pfft and kept creating.  Now they're the uncs and saying the same loopy stuff.  I just hope the new breed is giving them the same "pffft".

comments.author: Infinite-Switch6948
comments.body: yeah man this place is cool. I'm a professional muralist and there's a fairly strict no AI policy in my work, but i have always loved playing with technology and now I have been working in a game and dev tools since April and it's basically a dream come true.

comments.author: Middle-Moist
comments.body: Ive wanted to make games my whole life, well one game, but learning to code while supporting my family wasn't really an option. I have 0 prior skills in this area but for the first time ever I feel like that won't stop me from creating the game that has lived in my mind for over 2 decades. Its slow going, and frustrating at times bc I am pushing against what claude is used to. I enjoy this community for the same reasons, people here, by the large it seems, want to create and facilitate creation. I lurk mostly, but I genuinely appreciate that attitudes of those on this sub that know far more than I, and share that knowledge.

replies.author: NeusomaDev
replies.body: Same boat. Not for family reasons as much, but life being busy reasons. If you have a successful career and obligations in a totally different field, it's prohibitive to pick up all these different skills at a level of mastery that makes creating good games possible. Some people did it anyway before AI, and they truly deserve all the praise in the world. But man, there's plenty of us who had good ideas all along and just didn't have the means and opportunity to bring them to life. It's nice to be able to give it a shot finally.

comments.author: NeusomaDev
comments.body:
People always struggle massively to appreciate these things until they do something with it themselves. I completely understand why people instinctively resort to gatekeeping. I don't even think they're totally or even mostly wrong. When technology removes the effort bottleneck to producing trash but not the effort bottleneck to producing treasure, you get a proliferation of trash, and it's easy to blame the tech for enabling it. Much more rigid gatekeeping is clearly needed against slop of all kinds; what AI reveals is that, much like with security breaches recently, this vulnerability always existed, it just wasn't practically exploitable.

And yet, despite fully understanding and even agreeing with most of the complaints... I still find the doctrinaire reaction disgusting like you do. I understand that's the price of progress, and that those of us who think we're working on a genuinely great idea have the burden of proof. But they're so nasty and personal about it, and I don't know that I'll have it in my heart to forgive the haters if I ever do prove them wrong. I hope I'll be too happy enjoying the accomplishment to notice them quietly slipping into the party thru the back door.

comments.author: Creative-Donkey-1048
comments.body: I've spent years building tools to automate tedious gamedev tasks, but the real joy was in the messy trial-and-error of doing it the hard way first. the skills stuck, even if the code didn't.

comments.author: pugworthy
comments.body:
I developed software professionally for around 40 years, and have found AI to be incredibly powerful for coding in the right hands.   What I've seen is that experienced programmers can get it to shine for an incredible productivity boost.  Inexperienced programmers not so much.  Yes they can get it to do things, but they don't always make it shine.  That said, with the right LLM they can probably ask it to coach them and treat them like a junior programmer and mentor them.

With AI, you have to think more like an architect instead of just a programmer.  It's not "How do I implement X?" now.  It's "What do I need have implemented?" and "What is the intent or goal of this development effort?"  or even "I want to make X effect happen on the terrain surface, what's the best approach?"  It might suggest a shader implementation is the best way to manage something, and you've never written a shader - but it can.

It's like you're the senior tech lead sharing a cube with an incredibly fast developer next to you who will do what you ask, but also can learn and grow incredibly fast.  And they can offer you good advice and learn and do things you can't do.   You're talking with them, working with them, and prompts are a conversation where it's coding, you're trying out results, giving feedback, making adjustments, and so on.

comments.author: Odd_Cookie_3641
comments.body: I'm a senior dev, I've been working for 8 years and finally I can do games on my free time, I feel you 100%

comments.author: delicious_pubes
comments.body:
As a professional game dev, it’s an existential threat to our livelihoods and our ability to support our families. If you look at it that way it becomes much easier to understand many aren’t “gatekeeping” to feel special but are more afraid that the devaluing of the skills they built up over many years is going to cause them significant existential and financial harm. (Also their skills are being looked down on by some of the most mediocre slop peddlers I’ve ever seen so them being defensive makes sense there too)

I’m more inclined to lean in and accept that things are going this way and there’s nothing I can do so may as well enjoy it and hope that the adaptation will be fruitful, but I also understand my colleagues who either keep their head in the sand about how good models have gotten or choose to be “never AI” martyrs.

I’m happy that everyone has a chance to make games. I wouldn’t have been able to do it without the accessibility presented to me by RPG maker as a kid or Processing when I was a bit older and then Unity / Unreal when I was a hobbyist out of school. But if you weren’t putting in the real work to make something worthwhile before AI, then I wager you’re not putting the work in now either.

replies.author: asinglebit
replies.body: I understand the sentiment as im a software engineer as well. I write software to pay my bills. And i also dont know what future holds just like the next person. And I dont care how much effort people put in, effort is subjective theres no way of measuring it. Whats easy to you can be infinitely difficult for someone else due to neurological differences and a multitude of other factors. It is also naive to deny reality. The models are here, they are extremely good. They might get better, they might get worse. And im not saying its bad to do stuff without assistance of tools, theres beauty in that as well. Whats tiring to me personally is coming to places that once were inspiring to me - like programming and gamedev communities and see people turn their personal fears, beliefs and opinions into ideology

replies.author: delicious_pubes
replies.body:
Agreed. And I’m also tired of the pro-ai vs anti-ai culture war where neither side of the extreme really tries to consider why the other side feels the way they do and instead just villainize each other. 

I’m excited to see what creative people are making with the new models once the initial “oh my god look what I made in a week” posts are done and the people who have been heads down making amazing work start sharing.

It may be an existential threat, but I work full time and I’m a parent so being able to build this way is wonderful. I’m having as much fun making games now as I did when I first started many years ago when I had way more time and less responsibility.

replies.author: qualiadev
replies.body:
We are all in this boat. As a dev with 14 years experience (plus 2 CS degrees) these models are better than me. I know I’m more replaceable than I’ve ever been. In a year I don’t know where I’ll be, but I do know I’ve been able to bring ideas I’ve had my whole life to reality in a way that was never possible before. 

It’s a whole other question if those ideas were worth anything in the first place and whether people would ever pay me money for them but I know if this didn’t happen I would have never had the opportunity to try. Even though I would have been secure for a job for the rest of my life. I don’t know what reality I would prefer. Both are damning to me in different ways and I’d probably give you different answers. I’m sure if I lose my job I’ll be further to another side.
